The '''Morgan dollar''' is a [[United States dollar coin]] minted from 1878 to 1904, as well as 1921. It was minted again beginning in 2021 as a collectible. It was the first standard silver dollar minted since the passage of the [[Coinage Act of 1873]], which ended the [[Free silver|free coining of silver]] and the production of the previous design, the [[Seated Liberty dollar]]. It contained 412.5 [[Troy grains]] of 90% pure silver (or {{convert|371.25|gr|g ozt|adj=pre|Troy|disp=x| {{=}} |}} of pure silver). The coin is named after its designer, United States Mint Assistant Engraver [[George T. Morgan]]. The [[Obverse and reverse|obverse]] depicts a profile portrait representing [[Liberty (personification)|Liberty]], modeled by [[Anna Willess Williams]], while the reverse depicts an eagle with wings outstretched. The mint mark, if present, appears on the reverse above between D and O in "Dollar".

The dollar was authorized by the [[Bland–Allison Act]]. Following the passage of the 1873 act, mining interests lobbied to restore free silver, which would require the Mint to accept all silver presented to it and return it, struck into coin. Instead, the Bland–Allison Act was passed, which required the Treasury to purchase between two and four million dollars' worth of silver at market value to be coined into dollars each month. In 1890, the Bland–Allison Act was repealed by the [[Sherman Silver Purchase Act]], which required the Treasury to purchase {{convert|4500000|ozt|kg}} of silver each month, but only required further silver dollar production for one year. This act, once again, was repealed in 1893.

In 1898, Congress approved a bill that required all remaining bullion purchased under the Sherman Silver Purchase Act to be coined into silver dollars. When those silver reserves were depleted in 1904, the Mint ceased to strike the Morgan dollar. The [[Pittman Act]], passed in 1918, authorized the melting and recoining of millions of silver dollars. Pursuant to the act, Morgan dollars resumed mintage for one year in 1921. The design was replaced by the [[Peace dollar]] later the same year.

In the early 1960s, a large quantity of uncirculated Morgan dollars in their original bags were discovered in the Treasury vaults, including issues once thought rare. Individuals began purchasing large quantities of the pieces at face value and then [[Gresham's law|removed them from circulation through hoarding]], and eventually the Treasury ceased exchanging [[Silver certificate (United States)|silver certificates]] for silver coin. Beginning in the 1970s, the Treasury conducted a sale of silver dollars minted at the [[Carson City Mint]] through the [[General Services Administration]]. In 2006, Morgan's reverse design was used on a silver dollar issued to [[commemorative coin|commemorate]] the old [[San Francisco Mint]] building. The US Mint began striking Morgan Dollars again in 2021, initially as a commemorative to celebrate the 100th anniversary of the conclusion of the design's final usage, then as an annual release starting in 2023.

== Background ==

{{multiple image
| align     = left
| direction = horizontal
| total_width = 310
| image1    = Richard P. Bland_-_Brady-Handy.jpg
| alt1      = A photograph of a man wearing nineteenth-century formal clothing
| caption1  = In 1876, Richard P. Bland introduced a bill in the House to resume coinage of the standard silver dollar.
| image2 = William B. Allison_-_Brady-Handy.jpg
| alt2 = A photograph of a man wearing nineteenth-century formal clothing
| caption2 = William B. Allison added amendments to the bill in the Senate
}}

In 1873, [[United States Congress|Congress]] enacted the [[Coinage Act of 1873|Fourth Coinage Act]],{{sfn|Van Allen & Mallis|p=21}} which effectively ended the [[Bimetallism|bimetallic standard]] in the United States by demonetizing silver bullion.{{sfn|Fite|p=428}} Prior to enactment of the Coinage Act, silver could be brought to the mints and coined into legal tender for a small fee.{{sfn|Fite|p=429}} With such a system in place, bullion producers could have silver coined into dollars when the intrinsic value of a silver dollar was lower than the face value, thus making a profit, flooding the money supply and causing inflation.{{sfn|Van Allen & Mallis|p=23}} The act ended production of the standard silver dollar (then the [[Seated Liberty dollar]], as designed by [[Christian Gobrecht]]) and provided for mintage of a silver [[trade dollar (United States coin)|trade dollar]], which was intended to compete with Mexican dollars for use in the [[Orient]].{{sfn|Van Allen & Mallis|p=23}} Under the act, bullion producers were allowed to bring bullion to the mints in order to be cast into bars or coined into the newly authorized trade dollars for a [[Seigniorage|small fee]].{{sfn|Van Allen & Mallis|p=23}} Trade dollars initially held legal tender status, but it was revoked in 1876 to prevent bullion producers from making a profit by coining silver into trade dollars when the value of the metal was low.{{sfn|Yeoman|p=18}} The restrictions on free coinage laid out in the Coinage Act initially met little resistance from mining interests until the price of silver declined rapidly due to increased mining in the [[Western United States]].{{sfn|Fite|p=428}} Protests also came from bankers, manufacturers and farmers, who felt an increased money supply would have a positive impact. Groups were formed that demanded the free coinage of silver (or "[[free silver]]") in order to inflate the dollar following the [[Panic of 1873]].{{sfn|Van Allen & Mallis|p=24}}

Beginning in 1876, several bills were introduced in the [[United States House of Representatives|House of Representatives]] in an effort to resume the free coinage of silver.{{sfn|Van Allen & Mallis|p=24}} One such bill introduced into the House by Democratic Representative [[Richard P. Bland]] of Missouri was passed in the fall of 1876.{{sfn|Van Allen & Mallis|p=24}} Republican senator [[William B. Allison]] of Iowa added important amendments to the bill in the [[United States Senate|Senate]]. The House bill allowed Free Silver; one of Allison's amendments struck that provision.{{sfn|Van Allen & Mallis|p=24}} This same amendment allowed for the issuance of [[Silver certificate (United States)|silver certificates]] for the first time in United States history.{{sfn|Van Allen & Mallis|p=24}} The bill was [[veto]]ed by President [[Rutherford B. Hayes]].<ref name="Harness" /> The president's veto was overridden on February 28, 1878.<ref name="Harness" /> What came to be known as the [[Bland–Allison Act]] required that the Treasury purchase between two and four million dollars' worth of silver per month, to be coined into silver dollars at the former silver/gold value ratio of 16:1, meaning that one ounce of gold would be valued the same as sixteen ounces of silver.{{sfn|Fite|p=429}}

== Design history ==

{{multiple image
| align     = left
| direction = vertical
| image1    = Halfdollarmorgan.JPG
| width1    = 250
| alt1      = A pattern coin depicting a left-facing woman on the obverse and an eagle on the reverse
| caption1  = A pattern half dollar created by George T. Morgan
| image2    = 1878 Barber dollar coin pattern.jpg
| width2    = 250
| alt2      = A silver dollar pattern depicting a left-facing woman on the obverse and an eagle on the reverse
| caption2  = A pattern for the standard silver dollar created by William Barber
}}

In 1876, Director of the Mint [[Henry Linderman]] began efforts to redesign the nation's silver coins.{{sfn|Van Allen & Mallis|p=73}} Linderman contacted C.W. Fremantle, Deputy Master of the [[Royal Mint]] in London, requesting him to "find a first-class die-sinker who would be willing to take the position of Assistant Engraver at the [[Philadelphia Mint|Mint at Philadelphia]]."{{sfn|Van Allen & Mallis|p=73}} In response to Linderman's request, Fremantle wrote: "My inquiries as to an Assistant Engraver lead me very strongly to recommend for the post Mr. [[George T. Morgan|George Morgan]], age 30, who has made himself a considerable name, but for whom there is not much opening at present in this country."{{sfn|Van Allen & Mallis|p=73}} An agreement was reached between Linderman and Morgan for the engraver to work at the Philadelphia Mint under Chief Engraver [[William Barber (engraver)|William Barber]] on a six-month trial basis.{{sfn|Van Allen & Mallis|p=73}}

[[File:Anna Willess Williams 1892.jpg|thumb|upright|right|[[Anna Willess Williams]], Morgan's model for [[Liberty (goddess)|Liberty]], as depicted in an 1892 issue of ''[[Ladies' Home Journal]]'']]
Morgan arrived in Philadelphia on October 9, 1876.{{sfn|Van Allen & Mallis|p=73}} His earliest [[pattern coin]]s, designed during his tenure at the Philadelphia Mint, were intended for the [[Half dollar (United States coin)|half dollar]].{{sfn|Van Allen & Mallis|p=74}} In 1876, Morgan enrolled at the [[Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts]] to prepare to create a new [[Libertas|Liberty]] head design.{{sfn|Van Allen & Mallis|p=75}} Morgan also obtained studies from the nature of the bald eagle for the preparation of the reverse design.{{sfn|Van Allen & Mallis|p=75}} For the representation of Liberty, Morgan sought to depict an American woman rather than the usual Greek–style figures.{{sfn|Van Allen & Mallis|p=75}} Morgan's friend, artist [[Thomas Eakins]], suggested he use [[Anna Willess Williams]] of Philadelphia as a model.{{sfn|Van Allen & Mallis|p=75}} In total, Morgan had five sittings with Williams; he declared her profile to be the most perfect he had seen.{{sfn|Van Allen & Mallis|p=75}}

[[File:Morgan half dollar.jpg|thumb|left|alt=A coin depicting the profile of a young woman|Morgan's design, struck as a half dollar pattern in 1877]]
On October 18, 1877, Linderman requested Superintendent of the Philadelphia Mint [[James Pollock (American politician)|James Pollock]] to "instruct Mr. Morgan to prepare without delay, dies for a silver dollar, the designs, inscriptions, and arrangement thereof to be the same as the enclosed impression for the Half Dollar and numbered '2' substituting the words 'one dollar' in place of 'half dollar'". Linderman also ordered Pollock to "instruct Mr. Barber to prepare a reverse die for a dollar with a representation of an eagle as well as the inscriptions required by law. He will select whichever of his Heads of Liberty he prefers for the obverse of the same."{{sfn|Van Allen & Mallis|p=79}} Linderman evidently preferred the designs of Morgan over those of the Chief Engraver; he wrote Pollock on February 21, 1878, "I have now to state for your information, that it is my intention, in the event of the silver bill now pending in Congress, becoming law, to request the approval by the Secretary of the Treasury, of the dies prepared by Mr. Morgan."{{sfn|Van Allen & Mallis|p=83}}

== Production ==

[[File:Philadelphia, Mint coining press, from Robert N. Dennis collection of stereoscopic views cropped.jpg|thumb|alt=A photograph of a large machine used to strike coins|A coinage press at the Philadelphia Mint]]

Production of the coins did not commence until March&nbsp;11, more than a week after the passage of the Bland–Allison Act.{{sfn|Van Allen & Mallis|p=84}} The first acceptable strike, after adjustments to the press, was coined at 3:17&nbsp;p.m. at the [[Philadelphia Mint (II)|Philadelphia Mint]].{{sfn|Van Allen & Mallis|p=84}} This piece was given to President Hayes; the second and third were given to Secretary of the Treasury [[John Sherman]] and Mint Director Henry Linderman.{{sfn|Van Allen & Mallis|p=84}}

Linderman desired to involve the western mints of [[San Francisco Mint|San Francisco]] and [[Carson City Mint|Carson City]] in production in order to help reach the monthly quota necessary under the Bland–Allison Act.{{sfn|Van Allen & Mallis|p=86}} Pressure was so great at the Philadelphia Mint that it halted production of all other coins and began operating overtime.{{sfn|Van Allen & Mallis|p=88}} Use of the western mints was delayed, however, as all dies were prepared at the Philadelphia Mint, and it was believed that the Western mints did not have the proper equipment to prepare the dies for use.{{sfn|Van Allen & Mallis|p=87}} During the second week of production, Linderman pointed out what he called a "slight imperfection" in the dies for the dollar.{{sfn|Van Allen & Mallis|p=87}} The reason for the changes was to reduce the relief of the designs and to change the number of tail feathers on the eagle from eight to seven; this was done because all prior United States coinage depicted the bald eagle as having an odd number of tail feathers.{{sfn|Van Allen & Mallis|p=87}} The high relief had caused the dies to have a shorter life.{{sfn|Van Allen & Mallis|p=88}} Dies were eventually sent to the Western mints, arriving in both San Francisco and Carson City on April 16, 1878.{{sfn|Van Allen & Mallis|p=90}} The [[New Orleans Mint]] began striking the new silver dollars in 1879.{{sfn|Yeoman|p=219}}

The [[Denver Mint]], established in 1906, struck the coins for only one year, in 1921.{{sfn|Yeoman|p=221}} The [[mint mark]]s appearing on the coins are none, representing Philadelphia, "<small>CC</small>" for Carson City, "<small>S</small>" for San Francisco, "<small>O</small>" for New Orleans and "<small>D</small>" for Denver.{{sfn|Yeoman|p=221}} In order to conform to the Coinage Act of&nbsp;1837, the Morgan dollar contained ninety percent silver and ten percent copper, measured {{convert|38.1|mm|in|}} in diameter and weighed {{convert|412.5|gr|g}}.  Thus the pure silver content was {{convert|371.25|gr|g ozt|lk=in|adj=pre|Troy|disp=x| {{=}} |}}.{{sfn|Yeoman|p=218}}

===Key date===
The [[key date]] in the Morgan dollar series is the [[1893-S Morgan dollar]], which was struck at the United States [[San Francisco Mint]]. With a mintage of 100,000 coins struck, it is the lowest mintage of any Morgan Dollar. It is thought that few survived in [[mint state]] (MS) because the majority of the coins were in circulation.<ref name="NGC">{{cite web |title=1893 S $1 MS |url=https://www.ngccoin.com/coin-explorer/united-states/dollars/morgan-dollars-1878-1921/17226/1893-s-1-ms/ |website=NGC Coin |publisher=Numismatic Guaranty Company |access-date=11 September 2023}}</ref><ref name="Key Date">{{cite news |title=Key Date 1893-S Morgan Silver Dollar Offered at GreatCollections |url=https://coinweek.com/key-date-1893-s-morgan-silver-dollar-offered-at-greatcollections/ |access-date=11 September 2023 |publisher=Coin Week |date=31 May 2019}}</ref> In 2021 an 1893-S Morgan dollar in MS-67 sold for US$2,086,875.00.<ref name="Roach">{{cite news |last1=Roach |first1=Steve |title=Top 1893-S dollar brings series record $2,086,875 |url=https://www.coinworld.com/news/us-coins/top-1893-s-dollar-brings-series-record-2-086-875-dollars |access-date=11 September 2023 |publisher=Coin World |date=3 September 2021}}</ref>

== Sherman Silver Purchase Act, Panic of 1893 ==
{{main article|Sherman Silver Purchase Act|Panic of 1893}}
[[File:John-Sherman-2.jpg|thumb|upright=0.8|left|Ohio senator John Sherman authored the Sherman Silver Purchase Act, forcing the Treasury to purchase {{convert|4500000|ozt|kg}} each month.]]

Mintage of the Morgan dollar remained relatively steady until the passage of the Sherman Silver Purchase Act on July 14, 1890.{{sfn|Yeoman|p=220}} The act, authored by Ohio senator and former Treasury secretary John Sherman, forced the Treasury to increase the amount of silver purchased to {{convert|4500000|ozt|kg}} each month.{{sfn|Fite|p=446}} Supporters of the act believed that an increase in the amount of silver purchased would result in inflation, helping to relieve the nation's farmers.{{sfn|Van Allen & Mallis|p=27}} The act also received support from mining interests because such large purchases would cause the price of silver to rise and increase their profits.{{sfn|Van Allen & Mallis|p=27}} Despite the Act's requiring large purchases of silver indefinitely, it provided that the Mint must coin 2,000,000 silver dollars each month only until 1891.{{sfn|Van Allen & Mallis|p=29}} Minting of dollars dropped sharply beginning in 1892.{{sfn|Yeoman|p=222}} The silver that remained after mintage of the dollars was used to mint dimes, quarters and half dollars.{{sfn|Yeoman|p=220}}

Beginning early in 1893, a number of industrial firms, including the [[Philadelphia and Reading Railroad]] and the [[National Cordage Company]] went bankrupt.<ref name="Brothers pp48–52" /> The resulting bank runs and failures became known as the [[Panic of 1893]].<ref name="Brothers pp48–52" /> In June of that year, President [[Grover Cleveland]], who believed that the Panic was caused by the inflation generated by the Sherman Silver Purchase Act, called a [[special session]] of Congress in order to repeal it.{{sfn|Van Allen & Mallis|p=29}} The act was repealed on November 1, 1893.{{sfn|Van Allen & Mallis|p=29}} On June 13, 1898, Congress ordered the coining of all the remaining bullion purchased under the Sherman Silver Purchase Act into silver dollars.{{sfn|Van Allen & Mallis|p=29}} Silver dollar production rose again,{{sfn|Yeoman|p=221}} until the bullion was exhausted in 1904, when it ceased.{{sfn|Van Allen & Mallis|p=30}}

== Pittman Act ==
{{main article|Pittman Act}}
[[File:Key Pittman in 1915.jpg|thumb|right|upright|Senator Key Pittman was responsible for the act that called for the melting of up to 350,000,000 silver dollars.]]

The German government began a propaganda campaign during World War I to discredit the United Kingdom's currency in India.{{sfn|Van Allen & Mallis|p=30}} The Germans convinced Indian citizens that British banknotes in that country could not be redeemed for silver. This led to a run on the British supply of silver.{{sfn|Van Allen & Mallis|p=30}} In response, United States Democratic senator [[Key Pittman]] of Nevada introduced legislation in 1918 that was intended to offer financial relief to the British government.{{sfn|Van Allen & Mallis|p=31}} The bill, passed on April 22, 1918, stated that "sales of silver bullion under authority of this act may be made for the purpose of conserving the existing stock of gold in the United States, of providing silver for subsidiary coinage and for commercial use, and of assisting foreign governments at war with the enemies of the United States".{{sfn|Van Allen & Mallis|p=31}} The [[Pittman Act]] authorized the U.S. to melt up to 350,000,000 silver dollars,{{sfn|Van Allen & Mallis|p=31}} and this commenced immediately after the Act's passage.{{sfn|Van Allen & Mallis|p=31}} The U.S. eventually melted a total of 270,232,722&nbsp;silver dollars.{{sfn|Van Allen & Mallis|p=31}} Of that amount, 259,121,554&nbsp;were sold to the United Kingdom at the cost of one dollar per troy ounce.{{sfn|Van Allen & Mallis|p=31}}

The U.S. only minted the Morgan dollar again during 1921,{{sfn|Van Allen & Mallis|p=32}} the only year in which Morgan dollars were struck at the Denver mint. Since the Treasury had destroyed the obsolete Morgan dollar dies in 1910, Morgan had to create an entirely new master die.{{sfn|Van Allen & Mallis|p=95}} Another provision of the Pittman Act authorized the U.S. to mint a replacement coin for every silver dollar melted.{{sfn|Van Allen & Mallis|p=32}} During the same year, the [[Peace dollar]] was first issued to commemorate the end of [[World War I]].{{sfn|Yeoman|p=222}} The Peace dollar was approved to replace the outdated Morgan dollar design under the terms of the Pittman Act but without congressional authorization, despite the fact that the Act did not describe the coin design.{{sfn|Yeoman|p=222}} The change in design was actually authorized under an 1890 act of Congress,{{sfn|Van Allen & Mallis|p=409}} which stated:

{{blockquote | But no change in the design or die of any coin shall be made oftener than once in twenty-five years from and including the year of the first adoption of the design, model, die, or hub for the same coin:

''Provided'', That no change be made in the diameter of any coin:

''And provided further'', That nothing in this section shall prevent the adoption of new designs or models for devices or emblems already authorized for the standard silver dollar and the five-cent nickel piece as soon as practicable after the passage of this act.<ref name="Richardson pp806–807" />  }}

== Carson City Mint Morgan dollars  ==
Until 1964, U.S. citizens could redeem paper money known as [[Silver certificate (United States)|silver certificates]] for silver dollars at a U.S. Treasury mint on demand. In 1962, an individual redeemed a silver certificate and received a rare and valuable Morgan dollar in exchange. The coin was from a bag of silver dollars in the vault of the Philadelphia Mint.{{sfn|Yeoman|pp=27–28}}<ref name=gainesville>{{cite web|title=United States Mint Branch at Carson City, Nevada|url=http://www.gainesvillecoins.com/carson-city.aspx|access-date=4 September 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140905003747/http://www.gainesvillecoins.com/carson-city.aspx|archive-date=5 September 2014|url-status=dead}}</ref> This incident triggered huge interest, and between November 1962 and March 1964, millions of Morgan and Peace dollars were sold to the general public.{{sfn|Yeoman|pp=27–28}} The demand to exchange silver certificates for silver dollars was so great that lines formed outside of the Treasury Building in Washington, D.C. Some people in line were pushing wheelbarrows.{{sfn|Yeoman|pp=27–28}} The U.S. Treasury discovered previously unknown mint bags in its vaults containing slightly more than 2.8 million Carson City silver dollars.<ref name=gainesville/> Treasury officials decided to hold them back because the total number of coins minted at the Carson City mint were generally lower than others.{{sfn|Yeoman|pp=27–28}}

On May 12, 1969, the Joint Commission on Coinage held a meeting in order to determine the best way to sell the Carson City-minted dollars. They recommended a mail bid sale.{{sfn|Van Allen & Mallis|pp=397–402}} Legislation was passed on December 31, 1970, directing the Treasury to transfer the silver dollars to the Administrator of [[General Services Administration|General Services]] who was given the responsibility for marketing and selling the coins.<ref name="treasurysale" /> The legislation also stated that all proceeds from the sale were to be "covered into the Treasury as miscellaneous receipts."<ref name="treasurysale" /> Congress supplied the General Services Administration with $10 million to market the dollar coins.{{sfn|Van Allen & Mallis|pp=397–402}} Advertising consisted of posters and brochures distributed to post offices, banks and various financial institutions, as well as television documentaries.{{sfn|Van Allen & Mallis|pp=397–402}} The coins were sorted and mounted in small plastic display cases.{{sfn|Van Allen & Mallis|pp=397–402}} The GSA conducted a total of seven mail bid sales between 1972 and 1980.{{sfn|Van Allen & Mallis|pp=397–402}} In total, the sales generated $107&nbsp;million in revenue.{{sfn|Van Allen & Mallis|pp=397–402}}

Being about only 2% of Morgans were minted at Carson City, they demand a premium on the collector's market.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2024-11-18 |title=What is the GSA Hoard? - APMEX |url=https://learn.apmex.com/learning-guide/history/what-is-the-gsa-hoard/ |access-date=2026-09-21 |website=learn.apmex.com |language=en-US}}</ref>

== San Francisco commemorative dollar reverse==
[[File:SanFranciscoMintCommemorative.JPG|thumb|2006 commemorative silver dollar, bearing Morgan's reverse design with modifications]]

On June 15, 2006, legislation was approved that provided for the minting of a silver dollar and a [[Half Eagle|five dollar gold coin]] in "commemoration of the Old Mint at San Francisco," with surcharges to be given to the [[San Francisco Museum and Historical Society]] in an effort to rehabilitate the Old Mint.<ref name="commem" /> In total, 100,000&nbsp;gold and 500,000&nbsp;silver [[San Francisco Old Mint commemorative coins]] were authorized.<ref name="commem" /> Authorization came at the behest of several hobby publications, who enlisted readers to contact their local congressmen and persuade them to pass necessary legislation.{{sfn|Julian|p=265}} The approved designs include a frontal view of the Old Mint building on the obverse and a copy of Morgan's eagle design on the reverse.{{sfn|Julian|p=263}} Mint artist [[Joseph Menna]] made a new model for the reverse, employing a 1904 San Francisco-minted dollar as his model.<ref name="usmint" />

==Modern Morgan dollars==
[[File:2021 Morgan Commemorative Dollar Obverse.png|thumb|Obverse of the 2021 Morgan dollar]]
[[File:2021 Morgan Dollar in Display Box.jpg|thumb|2021 Morgan dollar in a United States Mint display box]]

On September 22, 2020, the U.S. House of Representatives passed legislation to allow the minting of Morgan and [[Peace dollar]] coins in 2021, the 100-year anniversary of the transition from the Morgan to Peace dollar in order to "commemorate this significant evolution of American Freedom".

House Bill 6192 (2021 Silver Dollar Coin Anniversary Act) allows production of Morgan and Silver dollars at 26.73g and no less than 90% silver ({{convert|24.057|g|ozt|abbr=on|disp=x| {{=}} |}}). On December 18, 2020, the United States Senate unanimously approved the bill, and it was signed into law by President [[Donald Trump]] on January 5, 2021. The [[Citizens Coinage Advisory Committee]] unanimously approved the design on January 19, 2021, with recommendations which were sent to the [[United States Secretary of the Treasury|Secretary of the Treasury]] [[Steven Mnuchin]], one day before the end of the Trump administration. There is no known mintage limit, and mintage could not begin until after January 1, 2021.<ref name="2021morganpeace" />

The [[US Mint]] then released order information for both dollars, priced at $85 apiece. Both coins are "0.858 [[troy oz]]. of .999 fine silver with an uncirculated finish"<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://catalog.usmint.gov/morgan-2021-silver-dollar-with-cc-privy-mark-21XC.html|title=Morgan 2021 Silver Dollar with CC Privy Mark |publisher=US Mint|access-date=2021-04-21|archive-date=2021-04-21 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210421211246/https://catalog.usmint.gov/morgan-2021-silver-dollar-with-cc-privy-mark-21XC.html|url-status=live}}</ref> Morgan Dollars were made available for purchase in May 2021, and sold out on the U.S. Mint website in 45 minutes, and had a staggered order window based on the different mint marks. [[Peace dollar|Peace Dollars]] were available beginning later in the same year. Each coin shipped in October 2021. High demand of these coins led to controversy over U.S. Mint ordering procedures and resulted in delays from the originally intended release dates. The 2021 Morgan Dollars were minted in the active mints of Philadelphia (no mint mark), Denver (D), and San Francisco (S). Two-thirds of the Philadelphia-minted dollars contained "[[privy mark]]s" for the now defunct Carson City (CC) and New Orleans (O) mints. The 2021 Peace Dollars had no mint mark and were only minted in Philadelphia.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://catalog.usmint.gov/peace-2021-silver-dollar-21XH.html |title=Peace 2021 Silver Dollar |publisher=US Mint|access-date=2021-04-21|archive-date=2021-04-21 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210421210546/https://catalog.usmint.gov/peace-2021-silver-dollar-21XH.html|url-status=live}}</ref> After the chaos caused by the CC and O dollars, the Household Order Limit was reduced from 10 to 3 for the remainder of the dollars.

The US Mint originally decided to continue the Morgan and Peace Dollar program for 2022 and beyond<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.coinworld.com/news/us-coins/morgan-and-peace-dollars-will-be-back-in-2022 |last1=Gilkes |first1=Paul |title=Morgan and Peace dollars will be back in 2022 |website=coinworld.com |date=2021-11-12 |publisher=Amos Media Company |access-date=2022-07-07 |archive-date=2022-07-13  |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220713205531/https://www.coinworld.com/news/us-coins/morgan-and-peace-dollars-will-be-back-in-2022 |url-status=live }}</ref> minted in San Francisco (S) with a [[Proof coinage|proof]] finish, but on March 14, 2022, announced that the planned 2022 releases had been scrapped due to "supply chain issues, production capacity and shipping logistics", and the rising price of silver, with plans to resume the program in 2023.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Gilkes |first1=Paul |date=Mar 18, 2022 |title=Mint officials cancel 2022 Morgan and Peace dollar production |url=https://www.coinworld.com/news/us-coins/mint-officials-cancel-2022-morgan-and-peace-dollar-production |website=coinworld.com |publisher=Amos Media Company |access-date=2022-03-25 |archive-date=2022-03-20  |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220320074852/https://www.coinworld.com/news/us-coins/mint-officials-cancel-2022-morgan-and-peace-dollar-production |url-status=live }}</ref>

For 2023, the US Mint announced plans to release Morgan Dollars in three finishes: [[Uncirculated coin|Uncirculated]], minted by the Philadelphia Mint with no mint mark, 275,000 mintage limit; [[Proof coinage|Proof]], minted by the San Francisco Mint with an S mint mark, 400,000 mintage limit; and [[Proof coinage|Reverse Proof]], released as part of a 2-coin set with a Peace Dollar, minted by the San Francisco Mint with an S mint mark, 250,000 mintage limit.

The 2023 Uncirculated Morgan Dollar was released by the US Mint on July 13, 2023, and sold out on the first day of issue.

== Mintage figures ==
[[File:Dollar-morgan.jpg|thumb|1881 Morgan Dollar Reverse]]

The dollars were produced every year between 1878 and 1904 at a total of four different mints. Each mint, with the exception of Philadelphia, has its own mint mark. In 1921 production was resumed for one year only, with this year being the only one where the Denver mint was used, until 2021.<ref>{{cite web |author=Ron Guth |url=http://www.coinfacts.com/silver_dollars/morgan_dollars/morgan_silver_dollars.html |title=Morgan Silver Dollars |website=Coinfacts.com |access-date=2017-10-30 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171020211107/http://www.coinfacts.com/silver_dollars/morgan_dollars/morgan_silver_dollars.html |archive-date=2017-10-20}}</ref> The number of dollars surviving are unknown as the Pittman Act resulted in the melting of millions of these coins, and the individual dates melted were never recorded. PCGS CoinFacts estimates survivals are less than 10% of the mintage.
